e.etymology: From Arminius, the Latin name of the Germanic chieftain who destroyed three Roman legions in AD 9; it may go back to a Germanic word for 'whole, great'. Armin is also a separate Persian name found in the Shahnameh.

assoc.t: Armin Arlert, strategist hero of Attack on Titan

e.etymology: From Arabic tahir, 'pure, virtuous', the active participle of a verb meaning 'to be pure'. Common across the Muslim world; Tahira is the feminine form.
From the English surname Isley. As a first name it rose in the 2010s alongside Isla and Paisley; the Isley Brothers made the surname famous in music.

assoc.t: The Isley Brothers, R&B and soul group

e.etymology: The English word, from Old French preisier, 'to value, to prize'. As a name it expresses praise to God and is especially common in Nigerian and other African Christian families.
Short form of Eugene, from Greek eugenes, 'well-born, noble', used as a full name in the US since the late 1800s. It has also served as a short form of Genevieve and Eugenia.

assoc.t: gene, the unit of heredity in DNA
Gene Belcher, the son in Bob's Burgers

e.etymology: A spelling of Kaylee, a modern English-language name that joins Kay and Lee. It was most used in the US around 2000.
The Italian and Latin name of Italy, given to girls in Italy as a patriotic name since the 1800s. The country's name is often traced to an ancient word for a land of young cattle.

assoc.t: Italia, the Italian name for Italy

e.etymology: A respelling of Hayden, an English surname from place names made of Old English heg, 'hay', and denu, 'valley', or dun, 'hill'.
A modern American spelling of Amari with the Ah- of Ahmad and Ahmir. Amari is itself a recent name of unsettled origin.
A spelling shared by several names: a form of the biblical Leah and of Leia, and a girl's name borrowed from Turkish and Arabic.

assoc.t: Princess Leia of Star Wars, whose name sounds the same

e.etymology: A Yiddish pet form of Chana, the Hebrew original of Hannah, from a root meaning 'grace, favor'. In the US it is used mainly in Hasidic and other Orthodox Jewish families.
e.note: The ch is the throaty Hebrew sound, so people who do not know the name tend to misread it as CHAY-nee.

e.etymology: From Greek Doris, 'woman of the Dorians', one of the peoples of ancient Greece. In myth Doris is a sea goddess, mother of the fifty Nereids. It came into regular English use at the end of the 19th century.

assoc.t: Doris Day, singer and 1950s film star

e.etymology: The French form of Margaret, from Greek margarites, 'pearl', borrowed into English in the 1860s. In French marguerite is also the word for the daisy.
namesakes: Marguerite Henry (author of Misty of Chincoteague)

e.meaning: cupped hands held in offering or greeting
e.etymology: From Sanskrit anjali, the gesture of hollowed or joined palms raised in offering, greeting and reverence. It is the hand position of the namaste greeting.

assoc.t: anjali mudra, the palms-together gesture in yoga

e.etymology: The Russian, Belarusian and South Slavic form of Maximus, Latin for 'greatest', which reached the Slavic world through Greek and the Orthodox church.
namesakes: Maksim Chmerkovskiy (Dancing with the Stars dancer)

e.etymology: The Hebrew form of Abigail, from av, 'father', and a root meaning 'to rejoice'. In the Bible Avigail is the wise wife of Nabal who later marries King David.
A spelling of Iliana, a Spanish variant of Ileana, a Romanian name thought to be a form of Helen. Iliana is also the Greek and Bulgarian feminine of their forms of Elijah.
A spelling of Arabic Rayyan, 'well-watered, luxuriant'. In Islamic tradition Ar-Rayyan is the gate of paradise reserved for those who fast.
The Spanish form of an Arabic name from the root for growth and increase, the feminine of Zayd. Zaida of Seville was an 11th-century Muslim princess who joined the court of Alfonso VI of Castile.
e.note: Zaida is also a common spelling of zayde, the Yiddish word for grandfather.

e.etymology: A Brazilian name of unclear origin that spread in the 2010s through the soccer star Neymar da Silva Santos Júnior, who was named after his father.
From Hindi and Urdu shaan, 'pride, dignity, splendor', a word that came from Arabic by way of Persian. Its sound is close to Sean and Shawn.
A Yiddish pet form of Esther, used mainly in Orthodox Jewish families. Esther, the biblical queen, has a name usually linked to the Persian word for star.

assoc.t: Esty Shapiro, heroine of Netflix's Unorthodox

e.note: Easily misread or autocorrected as Etsy, the online marketplace.

e.etymology: The English word, from Old English igland; the s crept in later through confusion with isle. As a name it follows Isla and nature names such as River and Ocean.
A modern name in the style of Maia, Kaia and Zaya. Zaia is also a traditional Assyrian man's name, borne by the early saint Mar Zaia.
A Kikuyu name and surname from Kenya, traditionally given to boys. In the US it is used for both girls and boys, alongside names such as Imani and Kamani.
A modern American elaboration of Aliyah with the -ana ending, also read as a spelling of Aliana.
A modern American compound of Lynn and Lee. It sounds the same as Linley, an English surname taken from a place name.
A respelling of Everly, an English surname from a place name made of Old English eofor, 'wild boar', and leah, 'woodland clearing'.
The French word for blue, used as an eye-catching spelling of the name Blue. English blue itself came from Old French bleu.

assoc.t: bleu cheese, as blue cheese is often spelled on menus
Bleu, R&B singer and rapper formerly known as Yung Bleu
Corbin Bleu, High School Musical actor (stage surname)

e.etymology: A recent American coinage in the family of Kamari and Kamani.
From Latin Christiana, the feminine of Christianus, 'follower of Christ'. Christiana is the heroine of the second part of John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress.

assoc.t: Christiana, Delaware, home of the Christiana Mall

e.etymology: From Sanskrit a-, 'not', and diti, 'bound': unbound, limitless. In the Vedas Aditi is the mother of the gods, the Adityas, and a personification of the infinite.
